title: "A Day In The Life Of A Hackathon Hacker Meet David Kay"
description: David Kay & Steven Jung work together to develop QUADRO, a drone autopilot equipped with voice commands and facial recognition.

asr.full_text: So the AR drone is a great product put out by a French company called Parrot and I had seen them. In the past before but never really driven one or flown one I guess or touched one or anything never. Been close to one until my friend Steven and I had this idea for the hack that we were. Going to buy him, figure out how to fly him on our own, and then try to take things to. The next level. In the past, I was working in medicine and had the idea to put voice recognition together. With medical visualization, so I did that maybe a month ago, and that was really interesting. But now, rather than working in medicine, my friend Steven is actually a former army. So we're exploring different ways that you might use a drone in the battlefield. So what if an individual soldier could send a drone ahead and scout for him rather than risk his own life by going into that tunnel or into that cave. So you'll see how we're putting voice control together with visual recognition to make this drone fly on its own and be kind of a pet for the soldier. Many challenges ahead. Number one challenge, can we read the camera, like at all? Like at all. Number two challenge, once we have the data, what do we do with it? Number three is can we recognize the judges faces? We'd love to be able to do. Facial recognition on the judges and say you know target identified, you know. Bradley Horowitz or something but we'll see. I've been coddled, you know a lot of. The younger generation of programmers grow up with the tools will take care of. A lot of these low-level issues for you and you know use Xcode, use Eclipse,. These high-level IDE environments will generate your make files for you. Now that we're writing them by hand it's getting a little bit more difficult. This is vital. Basically, if we can't get the camera feed up, then we're limited to a voice recognition driven drone and not a, what do you call it, not a drone that will be able to fly itself. Not a drone that can look around in this environment and identify a face and identify a person. So it's bad. It is 8.21 and man, things have not been going well. I was hoping that we could get the camera feed in from the drone into the Python programming language. And do all sorts of cool stuff with that, teach the drone how to fly itself around, recognize faces. But we're stuck in sea land. We're stuck in the low level binary code. It's now nearly midnight and we had a major crisis during the first half of the day. We weren't getting anywhere. We've made a breakthrough. So hopefully we can get everything together. And I guess I'll show you where we're at. Real quick update, Steven is training the voice model right now. So you might see him huddled in the corner, microphone up to the computer saying, you know,. Fly up, fly down, turn around, whatever. We use that to train the voice recognition model. And then I've got the camera feed just about there. So if we fire up the app, I'm actually building on a sample that comes from the manufacturer. We can see a live camera feed on the screen of what the drone here is looking at. So you can see my feet in front of the drone, kind of walking around. So that's the drone's point of view. And then here in the bottom right, this is the output from the program. So do I have this? Okay dude, I do have this hooked up. So I can now take off with the drone and again do another flight around the room. Although it looks like my controls are a little bit miscalibrated right now. I have a partner, Steven Jung, great guy. He's from San Diego, I'm from New York. I've actually been helping Steven pick up code on his way to jumping into startups. He's got a military background, worked in finance for a long time, now he's moving into. High tech and so we're kind of I guess consummating our relationship here at the Hackathon. But yeah, right. I've been to four Disrupt Hackathons I think. I've been to San Francisco 2010, New York 2011, New York 2012, and now San Francisco. 2012. As you can see here, we have some of our lunch still standing. That is going to be probably a 4 a.m. snack. Right now we're doing a full end-to-end test. We have our sound model in place. We've tested it with a microphone. Right now we just need to make sure that the voice commands are coming into the drone autopilot. And if that's working we're going to do a test flight with voice control. We have 15 minutes on the clock and counting. I think we might actually make it. I'm losing confidence but we'll see man, gotta give it your best. Run over and tell them man. Did you get it? Yes. So we barely just made the deadline. We've got 151 hacks we're going to show you today and each presenter, or group of presenters, has 60 seconds to present. Right now we're kind of refining our pitch. We're trying to get it to the point that we're going to be proud of it. Yeah? Okay. Mic me please. Who's next? Can you go next? You already did. Alright, great. The frightening truth is that drones are a reality. But as the average Army Ranger knows, often when you need them the most, they're too far. Away and maybe in someone else's hands, which is why we built Quadro, the personal drone,. A fully real-time voice recognition engine for Quadro. So Steven, without his hands, can give it flying instructions using only his voice. And this is a fully offline voice recognition model. Looks like we're getting a little out of control. I might need to bring it forward. Sorry about that guys. But this is a fully offline voice recognition model. One more time. Alright we're getting a malfunction here but not only have we built voice recognition... I'm devastated, well not devastated, I'm disappointed, right? Because we, it was a roller coaster, right? In the beginning of the Hackathon, the first day, it looked like we weren't going to get anywhere. And then we had a rally right around, you know, just before midnight, maybe like 9, 10, through midnight. And trucked on through the night, Stephen and I, and we got it to the point where the voice recognition was working,. Where the vision was working, we had everything working, but when we got on stage it was some. Sort of fluke, something fell apart and I couldn't diagnose it in 60 seconds on stage,. So we had to take what we could get. What really is going on here is just the level of complexity of the project that we undertook. Is on the higher side of things. Not to take anything away from any project out there, but certainly one small thing out. Of all the many things that we had to put together to make this thing actually work,. I'd say it's still a win. Two runners-up that get to go on stage and present for about a minute at Disrupt. On Wednesday at 1.45. Is Heat Data. And... Autopass? And Octopus? Octopus fell very strangely. So if you guys can come up. Come on down! The winner of this year's Hackathon in San Francisco 2012 is... We should just do this. Live ball! We did good. Next time I want to do great.

annotation.contextual_rationale: This video is non-scam content because it presents a hackathon project involving a drone autopilot controlled by voice commands and facial recognition. The content focuses on technical experimentation and a prototype demonstration, while the described presentation includes no request for payment, credentials, investment, or viewer participation.
annotation.fine_grained_rationale: The central content is programming, technical experimentation and an operational demonstration of a drone system, including voice-model training, camera-feed development and voice-command testing.
